verses.text: "Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber.
But the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep.
The gatekeeper opens the gate for him, and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
When he has brought out all his own, he goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him because they know his voice.
But they will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice."
Jesus spoke to them using this illustration, but they did not understand what He was telling them.
So He said to them again, "Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.
All who came before Me were thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them.
I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture.
The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
The hired hand is not the shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock.
The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,
just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep.
I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.
The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again.
No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father."
Again there was division among the Jews because of Jesus' message.
Many of them said, "He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?"
But others replied, "These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem. It was winter,
and Jesus was walking in the temple courts in Solomon's Colonnade.
So the Jews gathered around Him and demanded, "How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly."
"I already told you," Jesus replied, "but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father's name testify on My behalf.
But because you are not My sheep, you refuse to believe.
My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand.
My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father's hand.
I and the Father are one."
At this, the Jews again picked up stones to stone Him.
But Jesus responded, "I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?"
"We are not stoning You for any good work," said the Jews, "but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God."
Jesus replied, "Is it not written in your Law: 'I have said you are gods'?
If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and the Scripture cannot be broken—
then what about the One whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world? How then can you accuse Me of blasphemy for stating that I am the Son of God?
If I am not doing the works of My Father, then do not believe Me.
But if I am doing them, even though you do not believe Me, believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father."
At this, they tried again to seize Him, but He escaped their grasp.
Then Jesus went back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and He stayed there.
Many came to Him and said, "Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true."
And many in that place believed in Jesus.

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — a shepherding discourse that flows directly out of chapter 9's controversy, followed by escalating confrontation at two separate festivals
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: This chapter spans two distinct settings months apart: the immediate aftermath of chapter 9's controversy, and later the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) in winter, when Jesus walks in Solomon's Colonnade — a covered walkway on the temple's east side that would have offered real shelter from the cold.
context.custom: First-century Judean sheepfolds were often simple stone enclosures with a single narrow opening; at night the shepherd himself would frequently lie across that gap, literally becoming the door his sheep couldn't pass except through him. The Feast of Dedication commemorated the temple's rededication after the Maccabean revolt roughly two centuries earlier, when it had been defiled by pagan sacrifice — a meaningful backdrop for a chapter about who the "true" access to God's flock actually is.
context.timelineImmediate: This discourse follows directly from the previous chapter's expulsion of the healed blind man, with Jesus drawing a deliberate contrast between the religious leaders who just cast a man out and His own self-description as a shepherd who never abandons His sheep — a contrast that escalates months later at the Feast of Dedication into a direct claim of oneness with the Father and a second attempted stoning.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' shepherd imagery deliberately invokes Ezekiel 34's condemnation of Israel's failed shepherds and God's own promise to personally search for and gather His flock, while His claim "I and the Father are one" pushes His hearers to a response so severe — reaching for stones — that it confirms they understood exactly what He meant.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus describes Himself as both the gate sheep must enter through and the good shepherd who lays down His life for them willingly, in sharp contrast to hired hands who flee at the first sign of danger. Months later at the Feast of Dedication, pressed to state plainly whether He is the Christ, He answers with His boldest claim yet — "I and the Father are one" — and when accused of blasphemy, defends Himself by pointing directly to His own works before withdrawing safely across the Jordan.

translation.greek: ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (ho poimēn ho kalos)
translation.meaning: The word translated "good" here means more than morally good — it carries the sense of noble, genuine, the real thing as opposed to a counterfeit, directly contrasting Jesus with the "hired hand" described just after.

translation.greek: μία ποίμνη, εἷς ποιμήν (mia poimnē, heis poimēn)
translation.meaning: Jesus' reference to "other sheep not of this fold" points forward to Gentile believers eventually joining Jewish believers in a single unified flock — a major theme picked up throughout the rest of the New Testament.

translation.english: I and the Father are one
translation.greek: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν (egō kai ho Patēr hen esmen)
translation.meaning: The Greek word for "one" here is neuter, not masculine — grammatically pointing to unity of essence and purpose rather than Jesus claiming to literally be the same person as the Father.

otBackground.note: God's condemnation of Israel's failed shepherds and His promise to personally search for and gather His flock — directly behind Jesus' entire shepherd discourse.
"The LORD is my shepherd" — the most familiar Old Testament backdrop to Jesus' claim, "I am the good shepherd."
"I said, you are gods" — quoted directly by Jesus in His defense against the charge of blasphemy.

commentary.note: Henry notes the leaders demand a direct answer, 'not by parables... but totidem verbis — in so many words' — no more of the light-of-the-world or good-shepherd imagery, just a plain yes or no. He reads Jesus' response, 'I and my Father are one,' as denoting far more than agreement of purpose between two separate wills: 'it must be meant of the oneness of the nature of Father and Son, that they are the same in substance, and equal in power and glory.'

Henry observes that even without further theological debate, the reaction alone settles what Jesus meant: 'if we should altogether hold our peace concerning this sense of the words, even the stones which the Jews took up to cast at him would speak it out' — they clearly understood Him to be claiming full deity, and He never once denied that was His meaning.

Guzik draws on two older scholars for a precise grammatical point: 'one is neuter in gender, not masculine: the Father and the Son are not personally one, but essentially' (Alford); Trench put it even more directly — 'the word 'One' is neuter, and means one Essence: it is not masculine, which would have been one Person.' A small grammatical detail carrying real theological weight.

overview.summary: Jesus calls Himself the door and the good shepherd who lays down His life. At the Feast of Dedication in the temple He says His sheep hear His voice and that He and the Father are one, and some try to stone Him.
overview.settingLine: The temple, at the Feast of Dedication.

history.t: Hanukkah remembered the temple's rededication after the Maccabean revolt.
Prophets often called Israel's leaders shepherds, good or bad.

customs.t: At night several flocks shared a pen, and each sheep knew its own shepherd's voice.
A shepherd could lie across the pen's opening to guard it.

archaeology.t: The eastern wall of Herod's platform stands near where Solomon's Porch was.
Rock-cut folds and cisterns survive in the Judean hills.

overview.discussion: Jesus said His sheep know His voice. How do you recognize that voice among all the others?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
